African Swine Fever - What's the State Doing?

By: Liz Fish | Production

Proposal


Show:

Unique Selling Point:
African Swine Fever is a highly contagious and notifiable disease under the Animal Disease Act requiring the state veterinary services to intervene. The entire herd of pigs needs to be culled and their bodies disposed of and the farm or area quarantined, and then the State is required to compensate the farmer. But this hasn’t been happening. The State is slow to intervene and when they do they simply tests and confirm the presence of the ASF and will oversee the culling. They don’t insist the pigs be culled in order to avoid compensating the farmer. This has massive implications when pigs kept in townships and informal settlements like Mfuleni but also for commercial establishments which can keep up to 15 000 pigs.

Summary:
The GTG Fourie Piggery which has 15 000 pigs got ASF two months ago and the state apart from confirming the infection has done very little to assist. In desperation that took the Dr Mpho Maja as Director of Animal Health for the Department of Agriculture and Land Reform and Rural Development to court with an urgent application to fulfil their obligations under the Animal Diseases Act. The court ruled in GTG’s favour but instead and stepping up they maintain the court ruled they simply had to cover legal costs.
The implications of culling 15 000 pigs that have a commercial value of R50 million is massive. Once the infection is detected what do they do? It costs R120 000 a day to feed the pigs, and they now have no commercial value. If they stop feeding them they will eat each other and the farmers charged with cruelty to animals. They only have the facilities to dispose of 10% of the pigs and the Department are doing nothing except to insist the farm must be quarantined.


Further information:
ASF struck for the first time in the Western Cape in February this year in the informal settlement of Mfuleni. Since then no pigs have been allowed to leave the area, but of course they have been and there is a very real danger it could spread to the commercial farms in Paarl and Wellington. The NSPCA inspectors have been educating the farmers and have had to cull 274 pigs. The SA Pork Producers Association provided compensation to the farmers, not the state. NSPCA were never paid by the Department to do the job, or to dispose of the animals. All the Department veterinary services have done is provide a few syringes of disinfectant and when the NSPCA took the outcome of the GTG Fourie case up with the Department they denied it required them to take action, simply to oversee the culling. The situation is so dire in Mfuleni that if the pigs die and are buried in the area people dig them up to eat them. So restricting the sale and movement of pigs is an extremely difficult task and the GTG case study illustrates what a disaster it will be if it hits the commercial farms

Extra Budget Items:
GTG is in Potchestroom so that will be a 3 hour round trip and require a presenter for the whole day and SAPPA is also in Gauteng. Mfuleni is in Cape Town. It will require a return flight for both the presenter and the producer.

Press Release:


African Swine Fever Outbreak

African Swine Fever is highly contagious for pigs and it's spreading like wildfire across the country. First confirmed in the Western Cape in March, the Department of Agriculture, Land Reform and Rural Development and the Western Cape Agriculture Department jointly confirmed the outbreak. Carte Blanche tracks the outbreak all the way to North West where one farmer after the other suffers devastating financial loss as both emerging and commercial farmers are being wiped out. As farmers lose millions of rands worth of livestock, we ask: what is government doing to prevent further spread?

Producer: Liz Fish | Presenter: Masa Kekana

Watch the trailer

Script:


Script: African Swine Fever is hitting pig farmers hard across the globe, from China to Europe, and since 2016, has been on the rise in South Africa, with 27 outbreaks this year alone. It’s a virulent DNA virus which only attacks pigs, but with no vaccine or cure, pigs die within 24 to 48 hours of contracting it.

Link: African Swine fever is highly contagious for pigs but people can’t contract it or get ill from it, and the meat is perfectly safe to consume.
Script: People who have been in contact with sick pigs body fluids can transmit the virus. Pig farming has become extremely popular in informal settlements, and people can make a reasonable income feeding their pigs largely off restaurant waste.
In Mfuleni on the outskirts of Cape Town there are more than 200 pig farmers, with over 6000 pigs in a ¼ of square kilometre. Nomfundiso Ramba, has been farming pigs here for the last 20 years, earning about R20 000 a month, she says watching her pigs die, was too awful

Nomfundiso: It was very sad because when you saw the sick and those pigs, were making the noise like they they they cry and they were shaking

Script: African Swine Fever is a haemorrhagic disease, and notifiable under the Animal Disease Act, which requires the state to step in and cull sick animals to prevent the spread of the disease, and compensate the farmers. All 180 of Ramba’s pigs were destroyed
Nomfundiso: The mothers were sleeping next to the babies all dead. There were those pregnant ones CRYING

Script: In March the state with the assistance of the SPCA culled 270 pigs and removed them. Gary Buhrmann Chief State Vet for the Western Cape, says the state is unable to compensate the farmers

Gary: Well, basically the policy and the government at the moment just doesn't have to have money for compensation, quite a few of the farmers have got the covid support, the fifty thousand RAND food issue and there is also poppy support which they are also receiving

Script: The South African Pork Association stepped in and assisted the 5 farmers with a subsidy. The value of Ramba’s pigs was R200 000, she got R50 000 to help her survive

Link: At the beginning of the outbreak 5 farmers pigs were culled and removed and people were compensated now 3 months later it looks like people have been left to fend for themselves
Script: The SPCA Western Cape Chief Inspector Jaco Pieterse says he has had two inspectors working in the area everyday since February
Jaco “Ever since the outbreak of African swine fever in this area, the SPCA has humanely euthanized almost 400 further pigs that were sick and dying at our own expense. So it is spreading rapidly and something needs to be done now. The government needs to take control and they need to do their job.

Gary “we are in regular communication with the farmers, we on their whatsapp group if your pigs are dying in large numbers they let us know, and nobody has let us know. We can't have a technician in every single day because obviously there are other areas that have to be visited and once you've been in that area, you can't go to another area for at least 48 hours afterwards.

Masa: what can you categorically say you have done? Because these farmers say it's nothing so far they feel failed.

Gary: So we held a farmers day last week and the whole idea is training on biosecurity. How do you protect your pigs? We've supplied disinfectant 50 litres of concentrate, which is actually equivalent to sixteen thousand litres of disinfectant. we've supplying lime for the odd pigs that do die. Then they can bury them because it's not the numbers are not large enough to go in and actually cull out. We just feel that it's actually would be inhumane for four thousand healthy pigs

Script: But the SPCA inspectors painted a very different picture. Their records show that over 1000 pigs have died since March and they have had to euthanize a further 400 after the state cull.

Jaco: When the original culling took place and the state veterinary services took responsibility and they then removed the carcasses. But subsequent to that, pigs are dying on a daily basis and these farmers have nowhere else to go with the pigs and therefore they will simply dig a hole in the backyard amongst the other pigs and then they'll bury the pigs

Script: Linda Sicadi is unemployed and made R6000 a month from her pigs.

Masa: You had forty-five. And how many pigs do you have today?

Linda: Two piglets.

Masa: Two piglets.

Linda: within two weeks are gone., they told us they are not come to take this and they didn't tell us where we must dig. So we decided, OK, I must dig here I must dig there .

Masa: So in here you've got how many pigs buried

Linda: is 44 here

Script: Sicadi farms is just 50 meters from Adrian Koopman, he has 300 pigs and is hoping his biosecurity measures will protect him

Adrian: They are supposed to be a container that they can throw in the dead pigs. But there's no container there is nothing. And, uh, we also, .. use underground water and then you I don't think it's good to bury the dead, those pigs in the underground

Gary we don't have the infrastructure or the ability to actually remove the pigs. So with the site meeting we had with the Department and with Environment, they said they have no problem with them burying two or three pigs in an area

Script: The SPCA showed us 3 fresh mass graves, with of over 30 pigs in each, and the water table is just one and half meters down. People are dumping pigs in the canal and alongside the road

Lack of state capacity, and disposing of the dead pigs is a problem for both emerging and established farmers. African Swine Fever struck a commercial farm in Potchestroom on the 6th March

Link “We can’t go onto the farm because it’s under quarantine, but this farm has been under lockdown for two months and that means 17 000 animals are trapped in here
Deon:. It's extreme sadness and helplessness. there is nothing you can do and it's not going to go away.

Script: Deon Fourie farms with his father and brother, and says only 60 of the 17000 pigs were ill when ASF was detected
Deon: We had at least seven and a half thousand pigs that had not had contact with any of these sick animals. we should have been allowed to move those animals off the farm, they wouldn't allow us. They said it was too big a risk, even though we had tested them and that the animals were negative.

Link “A large commercial piggery is like a hospital, it has isolated sections so it’s possible if African swine fever is detected in one section and action is taken that the rest of the pigs can be saved
Script Johan Kotze CEO of the South African Pork Producers Association says when a disaster like this strikes swift action is critical

Johan: I think it's a difficult one to manage because of the capacity we have in government now in to deal with especially a big outbreak like what we have here. You can't go and barter and ask, you need to act. If you have a disaster, you go in, you manage the disaster.

Script. 4 weeks after the first case was detected, the whole farm of 17000 pigs was ill. Feed costs R120 000 a day, and they had no means of culling the animals on the farm. The state refused to step in and oversee the culling or the disposal of the carcasses. In the end they were forced to take them to court.

Deon: what the legislation says, all the infected animals and animals that have been in contact with them must be must be euthanized. But what it also says is that a representative of the state must be employed to oversee the action. And they were refusing to do that. They were saying anything we do is voluntary and sort of washing their hands clean of it.

Masa: That sounds very frustrating because it's already law.

Deon: Yeah, So us as farmers already under significant financial distress, had to pay an advocates and attorneys to take government to court to force them to do something that they knew they were supposed to be doing.

Script: They won their case and now the process of culling is underway, but its two months later and the state solutions of how to dispose of the bodies, is completely unworkable

Deon They didn't want to transport our pigs on a national road. Um, and these were healthy pigs that had tested negative that we could transport from here to an abattoir and slaughter them. Because of the situation we are in now where we have to mercy kill diseased animals, their answer put those pigs on a truck dead and bleeding and transport to Heidelberg and disposing there. The other remedy of maybe hiring a mobile abattoir. ..we must slaughter 30 pigs a day and it will take us 500 days to slaughter all of our pigs. they didn't give us any workable solutions.

Script: Director of Animal Health Dr Mpho Maja was unable to answer any questions about the situation on GTG Fourie piggery, citing section 25 of the Animal Disease Act which stipulates they cannot discuss individual farmers information

Script: The farmer is R80 million down and ran out of money to feed the pigs, SAPPO stepped in , and is also assisting with the culling alongside the State and SPCA. But they have to compost 17 000 animals on the farm.

Deon: So as long as they didn't give the instruction and we did it on our own, they would know there would be no claim for compensation. There's no way we could start again. The 85 jobs that are lost will remain lost. The farm will stand empty. So we are desperate to get compensated just so we can carry on going.

Johan: that's what's devastating, you can't you can't have an outbreak, and it's day 60 today. And you still we just halfway through the process of depopulating this farm, it should have happened day three, four or five out of an outbreak.

Script And in Mfuleni the State is also fumbling, the disease is spreading with new cases reported in Somerset West. And the farmers who have had all their pigs culled can’t start over, because the disease is far -from under control

It costs R120 000 a day to feed the pigs, and they now have no commercial value. If they stop feeding them they will eat each other and the farmers charged with cruelty to animals. They only have the facilities to dispose of 10% of the pigs and the Department are doing nothing except to insist the farm must be quarantined.
metadata.Further information: ASF struck for the first time in the Western Cape in February this year in the informal settlement of Mfuleni. Since then no pigs have been allowed to leave the area, but of course they have been and there is a very real danger it could spread to the commercial farms in Paarl and Wellington. The NSPCA inspectors have been educating the farmers and have had to cull 274 pigs. The SA Pork Producers Association provided compensation to the farmers, not the state. NSPCA were never paid by the Department to do the job, or to dispose of the animals. All the Department veterinary services have done is provide a few syringes of disinfectant and when the NSPCA took the outcome of the GTG Fourie case up with the Department they denied it required them to take action, simply to oversee the culling. The situation is so dire in Mfuleni that if the pigs die and are buried in the area people dig them up to eat them. So restricting the sale and movement of pigs is an extremely difficult task and the GTG case study illustrates what a disaster it will be if it hits the commercial farms
